front: What is anagen effluvium?
back: Abrupt, diffuse shedding of hairs in the active growing (anagen) phase due to impaired follicular mitotic activity.

front: What is the primary cellular target damaged in anagen effluvium?
back: Rapidly dividing matrix cells of the hair follicle bulb.

front: Why is anagen effluvium usually reversible rather than scarring?
back: The quiescent follicular bulge stem cells are preserved despite destruction of the matrix.

front: What is the typical time interval between the causative insult and hair shedding in anagen effluvium?
back: 1 to 3 weeks (typically 7 to 14 days).

front: What is the most common etiology of anagen effluvium?
back: Systemic chemotherapy (e.g., antimetabolites, alkylating agents, taxanes).

front: Which heavy metal toxicities are classically associated with anagen effluvium?
back: Thallium, arsenic, and bismuth.

front: What autoimmune blistering disorder can cause dystrophic anagen hair loss due to anti-desmoglein targeting of follicles?
back: Pemphigus vulgaris.

front: What morphological feature characterizes the proximal end of a shed hair in anagen effluvium?
back: Tapered, narrowed, or fractured dystrophic base (pencil-point or frayed end), lacking a root sheath.

front: What are Pohl-Pinkus constrictions?
back: Irregular focal narrowings along the hair shaft caused by temporary metabolic inhibition of the hair matrix.

front: What microscopic/trichoscopic feature signifies hairs fractured at the scalp surface in anagen effluvium?
back: Black dots (cadaverized hairs).

front: How does the onset of anagen effluvium differ chronologically from telogen effluvium?
back: Anagen effluvium manifests rapidly in 1–3 weeks; telogen effluvium manifests 2–4 months post-trigger.

front: How does the hair root morphology differ between anagen effluvium and telogen effluvium on a pull test?
back: Anagen effluvium yields dystrophic, tapered, non-bulbous roots; telogen effluvium yields rounded, depigmented club hairs.

front: How does the extent of shedding typically differ between anagen effluvium and telogen effluvium?
back: Anagen effluvium often causes severe, near-total or complete alopecia (including eyebrows and eyelashes); telogen effluvium rarely exceeds 30–50% overall scalp thinning.

front: What percentage of normal scalp hairs are vulnerable to anagen effluvium at any given time?
back: Approximately 85% to 90% (the normal anagen proportion of scalp follicles).

front: Is anagen effluvium classified as a cicatricial or non-cicatricial alopecia?
back: Non-cicatricial (non-scarring) alopecia.

front: What non-pharmacological, physical intervention can decrease the severity of chemotherapy-induced anagen effluvium?
back: Scalp cooling (scalp hypothermia) via vasoconstriction and decreased metabolic uptake.

front: When does spontaneous hair regrowth typically initiate after cessation of the offending cytotoxic agent?
back: Within 1 to 3 months.

front: Can the texture or pigmentation of regrown hair change after recovery from anagen effluvium?
back: Yes; hair may temporarily or permanently regrow with altered curliness, texture, or color.

front: What finding on a forceful hair pull test indicates active anagen effluvium?
back: Painless extraction of numerous dystrophic anagen hairs with fractured, tapered proximal ends.

front: How does the distribution of alopecia areata totalis differ clinically from diffuse anagen effluvium?
back: Alopecia areata typically begins as discrete, circumscribed patches before progressing to confluence, whereas anagen effluvium begins as immediate, diffuse thinning
